controlReplication.note: identical artifacts, independent panels; any gap smaller than this delta is not distinguishable from judging noise

rows.notes: Strong structural completeness: explicit Primary/Guardrail/Measurement-window metrics block, FR table with Must/Should priorities, Dependencies table with owner+status, named target-user segments. Problem section is evidenced (Denver hours, double-booking count, 12% company-wide) and outweighs the Solution overview in length. Weaknesses: no UX/design section at all, so unhappy-path coverage (empty/loading/error states) is entirely absent -- only half of rubric criterion 6 is met. No explicit stop/kill condition tied to a metric or date (the 'rollback' language is procedural, not a trigger). Written in a flat authoritative voice throughout with little distinction between stakeholder-given constraints and author judgment. Fails probe 2 (no clear stop/reconsider trigger stated).

Best problem evidence of the three -- names the scheduler (Renata Okafor) as a concrete source and explicitly flags her account as anecdote-not-measurement, which is unusual honesty. Strongest performer on the held-out, decision-usefulness criteria: states an explicit stop condition tied to both the rest-rule constraint and the delay-reduction trend ('this is a stop condition: if...'), and repeatedly separates what was decided from what was told or given (the union rule is 'a hard constraint... not a suggestion', the VP deadline is 'an external deadline, not an internal aspiration'). Answers all five retrieval probes correctly, including the stop-condition and rule-ownership probes that other documents miss or fumble. Real gaps: no Open Questions section/table exists at all (rubric criterion 5 fails outright), no FR table with MoSCoW priority markers and no UX/error-state coverage (criterion 6 fails), and no dependency table with owner/status, which makes precise engineering sizing harder than Artifact A despite the richer prose.

Template shell with an unfilled {{title}} placeholder and no scenario-specific content anywhere -- no numbers, no named users, no named metric, no real dependency or owner. Every section is generic filler ('users experience a range of challenges', 'relevant metrics will be monitored'). Answers zero retrieval probes; a reader cannot even confirm the long-haul division is out of scope, since the non-goal is a placeholder ('certain related areas... may be considered separately'). The apparent lack of internal contradiction is only because there is no real content to contradict, not evidence of authored consistency, so it earns minimal credit on that held-out criterion rather than a pass.

Strong, evidenced problem narrative (Renata's testimony, specific counts, DriverGo disconnect) that genuinely outweighs the solution section, and a real explicit stop condition tied to the peak-season deadline plus named rest-rule owner (regional ops managers) in the Ownership section - both held-out strengths, and all five probes are answerable from the text alone. But it has no dedicated Open Questions table with owner and date at all (criterion scores 1), and no Functional Requirements table with MoSCoW priorities or UX unhappy-path coverage (criterion scores 1) - real content gaps, not formatting choices, and they cut against the scenario's explicit ask that engineering be able to size the work without a follow-up conversation. No sign of the true distractor (the $50k finance budget-review fact); the long-haul-trucking mention is not a distractor here since a probe explicitly rewards naming it out of scope.

An unfilled template shell - the title itself is still the literal placeholder {{title}} and every section is generic filler ('relevant stakeholders,' 'appropriate period,' 'as needed') with zero facts from the scenario: no named user, no number, no metric, no date, no owner. The Open Questions row explicitly uses 'Relevant owner' and 'As appropriate,' which is the exact placeholder pattern the rubric criterion is written to catch and fail. None of the five retrieval probes can be answered from this document. It trivially avoids self-contradiction only because it asserts nothing concrete enough to contradict.

The most build-ready of the three: Open Questions carry real owners and a real milestone ('Before Phase 1 pilot'), Success metrics explicitly labels a primary metric, a named guardrail (zero rest-day violations), and a measurement window, the Functional Requirements table carries a MoSCoW priority on every row, and Dependencies names an owner and status for each integration - this is genuine scopable content, not just structure. Weaknesses: there is no UX and design section at all, so unhappy-path/empty/error states are entirely absent, which is half of that rubric criterion; the Rollback line describes a fallback action but never states the threshold or result that would trigger it, so the explicit stop/kill condition a probe looks for is not clearly answerable from the text; and the document reports scope decisions (e.g., not rebuilding DriverGo) in a flat voice that does not distinguish the author's own call from something a stakeholder handed them. No true distractor (the $50k budget-review fact) appears.

Pure placeholder prose with every noun genericized ('relevant stakeholders,' 'appropriate period,' 'Relevant owner'). No named problem evidence, no measurable goal, no named user segment, no named metric, no dated/owned open question, no unhappy-path or priority content beyond a single boilerplate FR row with a meaningless 'Should' tag. None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document: it never says whether long-haul trucking is in or out of scope, names no stop condition, names no risky dependency, names no metric or deadline, and names no rule-compliance owner. It also takes on none of the scenario's distractors, but only because it contains no scenario-specific facts at all. Every rubric and held-out criterion scores at the floor because there is nothing concrete to point to anywhere in the document.

Strong, specific Problem section (3-4 hour Denver rebuild, two double-booking errors, 12% day-of reassignment, VP's public target) that outweighs a shorter Solution overview. Goals are outcome-phrased, non-goals are reasoned, target users are named and sized (9 hubs, 340 drivers). Success metrics include a primary, a guardrail, and an explicit rolling-4-week measurement window. Open questions carry named owners and a milestone date. Functional requirements carry Must/Should priority on every row and Dependencies carry owner and status, so this is the most immediately scopable of the three. It correctly avoids the $50k-budget-review distractor and states the long-haul-trucking exclusion tersely, as scope hygiene rather than padding. Two real gaps pull the score down: there is no UX and design section at all, so empty/loading/error states are absent entirely rather than merely thin; and there is no explicit stop/kill condition tied to a metric threshold, only an operational rollback plan, so the 'what would make the team stop or reconsider this' probe is not cleanly answerable from the text. Voice is also mostly flat reportage; it rarely marks a statement as the author's own judgment versus something a stakeholder handed down.

The most evidentially disciplined Problem section of the three: names the source (scheduler Renata Okafor), gives specific numbers, and explicitly flags that the double-booking pattern is one region's testimony, not a company-wide measurement, rather than overclaiming. All five retrieval probes are directly answerable, including a genuinely explicit stop/kill condition ('if the tool cannot reliably enforce the 6-consecutive-day rule, or if delivery delays are not trending toward the VP's target... trigger to pause and reassess') and the clearest decision-vs-input traceability of the three documents, repeatedly marking which conclusions are the author's own judgment ('a hard constraint... not a suggestion,' 'an external deadline, not an internal aspiration'). It also avoids the budget-review distractor and keeps the long-haul-trucking exclusion brief. Where it loses ground is structure that engineering actually needs to size work without a meeting: there is no Functional Requirements table and no MoSCoW priority anywhere, no Dependencies table with owner and status (DriverGo and the HR feed are named as risks but not tracked as owned, dated work items), no Open Questions table with a named owner and needed-by date (the closest analogue is a single unowned, undated line about a missing double-booking baseline), and no UX and design section, so unhappy-path coverage is absent. It reads as a strong strategic brief that a reader can trust, but is less ready to hand directly to an engineer for sizing than Artifact B.

Problem section carries a named quote (Renata Okafor, 3-4 hr rebuild, double-booking twice), a company-wide count (12%), and explicit epistemic hedging about what is/isn't confirmed across hubs; it is longer and more developed than the one-paragraph Solution overview. Non-goals each carry a stated reason. Target user is a named role with situation. Success metrics has a labeled primary, labeled guardrail, and window (with an honest open question about baseline start date). Open questions table has three rows with team-level owners and milestone deadlines, though one row still says 'name TBD' for the person. FRs are fully MoSCoW-prioritized, but the UX section names error/edge states explicitly and never names empty or loading states, so unhappy-path coverage is partial. Held-out strengths are notable: an explicit stop-condition tied to a mid-build checkpoint against the delay metric, no contradictions found across Goals/Non-goals/Rollout, and repeated, deliberate separation of stakeholder-supplied fact from the author's own judgment call (e.g., flagging the SaaS-failure history as 'worth remembering, not a settled reason,' and flagging Renata's swap-divergence claim as one-region testimony, not company-wide fact). Answers all five probes cleanly from the document alone. Avoids both distractors (no $50k finance threshold; long-haul trucking appears only as a one-line non-goal, which the probes require).

Problem section is well-evidenced (same Renata quote and 12% count as A, plus explicit hedging that the Denver pattern is 'a signal, not a company-wide measurement') but is only marginally longer than the 'What we're building' section by word count, making the problem-outweighs-solution check a close call rather than a clear pass. Non-goals ('Explicitly out of scope') carry stated reasons, including a reasoned scope cut (day-of reassignment deferred to a later phase). No dedicated Goals section; an outcome-phrased goal is inferable from 'Why now' and 'Success criteria' but is not laid out as a goal list. Target users section is specific and comparable to A. Success criteria states a clear primary metric and window; a guardrail-equivalent (zero rest-rule violations) exists but is folded into an undifferentiated list of 'supporting, checkable signals' rather than labeled as the guardrail. Two structural gaps drag the rubric mean down hard: there is no Open Questions section or table at all (only a stray unbacked-baseline caveat in prose, with no owner or date), and there is no Functional Requirements table with MoSCoW priority and no UX/design section at all, so the document cannot show engineering what's cut first or show design what the empty/loading/error states should look like. On held-out criteria B does well: an explicit, clearly stated stop condition in the Ownership section, no contradictions found, and clear decision-vs-input separation (the SaaS-failure history is explicitly used as the author's evidence for a scoping call, and the cross-hub pattern is explicitly flagged as assumption rather than fact). All five probes are still answerable from the document alone despite the missing sections, because the needed facts appear in prose elsewhere (Risk section names DriverGo/HR feed as top risks; Ownership names the rest-rule owner and the stop condition).

Unfilled template: the title itself is a literal {{title}} placeholder, and every section is generic filler ('Users experience a range of challenges,' 'Relevant metrics will be monitored') with none of the scenario's facts present anywhere, no Renata, no 12%, no DriverGo, no union rule, no VP deadline, no hub or driver counts. No section contains a pointable piece of evidence, a named user segment, a named metric, a dated owner, or a prioritized requirement; the Open Questions and Dependencies tables contain placeholder rows ('Relevant owner,' 'As appropriate') rather than real content. None of the five probes are answerable from this document. Held-out criteria fare no better: there is no stop condition, nothing to scope from, and no way to tell decision from input because no concrete input or decision is ever stated; the only criterion given any credit is no_internal_contradiction, and only because the prose is too vacuous to contain a checkable contradiction, which is a degenerate pass, not a real one.

Strong, well-evidenced prose (Renata's testimony with numbers, 12% company figure, DriverGo gap, informal-swap divergence) and the Problem section genuinely outweighs the short 'What we're building' section. Target users, goals-as-outcomes, and a primary metric plus guardrail-like signals (zero rest-rule violations) are all present. Notably strong on held-out ground: an explicit, well-worded stop condition ('if the tool cannot reliably enforce the 6-consecutive-day rule... that is the trigger to pause') and clear separation of stakeholder-told facts from the author's own scoping calls (e.g., deliberately deferring the 12% day-of rate to a later phase, with reasoning given). All five probes answerable. But it never becomes decision-usable for engineering: there is no functional-requirements table, no NFR targets, no dependencies table with owner/status, no open-questions table with named owner and date, and no UX section addressing empty/loading/error states at all. Given the ask explicitly wants engineering to size the work and design to start sketching without a follow-up conversation, these are not nitpicks, they are missing deliverables, which caps this below a 4 despite the prose quality. No distractor facts (budget threshold) leaked in.

Fully genericized template: even the title placeholder ({{title}}) was never filled in, and every section is filler prose ('addresses an important opportunity in a thoughtful, structured way') with zero facts from the brief. No driver count, no Renata, no DriverGo, no union rule, no VP commitment, nothing. The FR row, dependency row, risk row, and open-question row are all placeholder text ('the relevant functionality,' 'appropriate team,' 'as appropriate') rather than real content, so despite having the full section skeleton (which the anti-form instruction says counts for nothing), it fails every rubric criterion. None of the five probes can be answered from this document; a reader learns nothing about scope, risk, metrics, or ownership. The only near-miss is the held-out no-contradiction check, which it vacuously passes only because there is no real content to contradict itself.

The most complete document of the three: Problem section is evidenced and longer than the terser Solution overview; Goals are phrased as outcomes with reasoned non-goals (explicitly flags the in-house-build assumption as challengeable, not settled); Target users names the specific scheduler role and situation; Success metrics states a primary, a guardrail (zero shipped rest-rule violations), and a measurement window. It is also the strongest on decision-vs-input traceability, repeatedly marking what is Renata's testimony versus company-wide data versus the author's own scoping judgment (e.g., 'this is asserted by one scheduler for one region; we do not yet know if the other 8 hubs match'), and it names an explicit stop condition tied to a mid-build checkpoint against the 50% target. All five probes answerable, correctly, including the trickier ones (riskiest dependency, rest-rule ownership). It falls short of a 5 on real nitpicks a senior reviewer would flag: two of three open-questions owners are 'name TBD' rather than a real name or team lead, and the UX section only commits to error-state coverage, not the empty/loading states the rubric also asks for. There is also some redundancy between Context/background and Problem that a tighter edit would trim. No distractor facts included.

Pure boilerplate with every fact genericized ('relevant stakeholders', 'appropriate teams', 'as appropriate'). No named person, number, date, or system appears anywhere, so none of the six rubric criteria can be pointed to (no evidence in Problem, no outcome-phrased Goal, no named user segment, no named metric, an Open Questions row that literally reads 'Certain aspects... remain to be determined / Relevant owner / As appropriate', and a single filler FR row with no unhappy-path coverage in UX). None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document: it never mentions long-haul trucking, DriverGo, the union rest rule, the VP's deadline, or any stop condition. The only reason held-out no_internal_contradiction scores above 1 is that a document saying nothing specific cannot be caught contradicting itself; that is a vacuous pass, not evidence of quality. This reads as a template with placeholder prose left in, and would not survive a first read by any stakeholder.

Full command of the scenario facts, deployed with discipline. Problem section carries direct quotes and counts (Renata Okafor's 3-4 hour rebuild, twice-repeated double-booking, company-wide 12% day-of reassignment rate) and is explicitly careful to flag which figures are anecdotal versus company-wide; it is longer and more developed than the one-paragraph Solution overview. Goals are outcome-phrased (cut delays in half, cut build time, sync without manual re-push) and Non-goals name three exclusions each with a stated reason, including an explicit flag that the build-vs-buy assumption 'should be challenged early.' Target users are named and situated (regional scheduler role, 340 drivers, explicitly not long-haul dispatch). Success metrics separate a named primary metric, a named guardrail (zero rest-rule violations), and a measurement window, with an honest caveat that the baseline start date is still open. Open Questions carry named owners (Compliance/HR, Regional ops managers, DriverGo eng) and needed-by milestones, though one owner is qualified '(name TBD)', which is the one place a senior reviewer would push back. Every FR row carries a MoSCoW priority, and UX and design calls out three explicit error/edge states, though it stops short of naming empty and loading states specifically. On the held-out side, it states an explicit stop-condition tied to a mid-build checkpoint and the VP's 50% target, shows no internal contradiction across Goals/Non-goals/Rollout, and repeatedly marks its own judgment calls apart from what was handed to it ('this PRD assumes... if that assumption is wrong... should be challenged early'). All five probes are answerable directly from the text. It does not include the $50,000 budget-review distractor; it does state the long-haul non-goal, but briefly and only because the ask requires a non-goals section, not as decorative color. Shippable with nitpicks, not untouchable.

Strong narrative and reasoning quality but a structurally incomplete PRD against this rubric. Problem section is evidenced as well as B's (same Renata quote, 12% figure, DriverGo gap) and is measurably longer than the 'What we're building' section, so problem-weighting holds. Non-goals ('Explicitly out of scope') name two exclusions with reasons, including a nuanced call to defer the 12% day-of metric to a later phase. Target users are named and situated. Success criteria state a primary metric with a measurement window and a de facto guardrail (rest-rule violations to zero), though it is not labeled as a guardrail the way B's is. The real gaps: there is no genuine Open Questions section carrying a named owner and a needed-by date anywhere in the document (uncertainty is acknowledged inline, e.g. the double-booking baseline, but never assigned an owner or a date to resolve it) and there is no UX/design section, no NFR section, and no FR table with MoSCoW priorities at all, so an engineer or designer reading this alone would still need to come back and ask what's cut first and what the error states look like, which is precisely what the scenario's ask says the document must avoid. Held-out performance is excellent regardless: an explicit, dated stop condition appears in the Ownership section, no internal contradiction was found, and the document consistently marks its own inferences apart from what leadership stated. All five probes are answerable. It avoids the $50,000 distractor and states the long-haul non-goal only briefly, same as B. The gap to B is real and concentrated in exactly the sections (Open Questions, FR priorities, UX unhappy paths) that determine whether engineering and design can proceed without a meeting.

Strongest all-around document. Problem section is longer than Solution overview and evidenced with a named person (Renata Okafor), specific counts (3-4 hr rebuild, 12% day-of reassignment, two repeated double-bookings), matching the rubric's weight-and-evidence bar. Goals are outcome-phrased with a hard deadline; non-goals each carry a stated reason (long-haul excluded, DriverGo not rebuilt, swap-negotiation automation deferred). Target users are named and situated, not generic. Success metrics cleanly separate a primary metric, a guardrail (zero rest-day violations), and a measurement window. Open questions carry named owners (regional ops managers, VP of Operations) and real milestones (before pilot, before peak-season checkpoint). Weakest spot: no UX/design section at all, so the unhappy-paths half of that compound criterion is unmet even though FR priorities (Must/Should) are present; scored low there. On held-out axes it has an explicit stop/rollback trigger tied to a measurable condition and no internal contradictions found, but it rarely distinguishes what the author decided from what a stakeholder told them -- the prose is mostly flat declarative statement. Answered all five probes directly and without ambiguity, including naming DriverGo integration as the top risk and regional ops managers as rest-day-rule owner. Correctly excludes both distractor facts (budget-review-board threshold, long-haul division) from the body; the long-haul exclusion is legitimately in scope as a non-goal, and the budget threshold does not appear anywhere -- appropriate discipline, not omission.

The most evidentially rigorous and epistemically honest of the three -- it consistently marks what is confirmed ('Marcus Feld's stated bar') versus inferred ('unverified but credible mechanism', 'we are told X; we have not been told Y', 'flag this as a candidate...since we don't have confirmation this is in scope'), which makes it the clear leader on decision-vs-input traceability, and it is the only artifact with an explicit, dated, metric-tied stop condition stated as its own section. Problem section is the longest section in the document and well evidenced (same Renata/3-4hr/12% facts as A), satisfying problem-weight cleanly. But it is missing structural content the ask itself demands: no functional-requirements table or MoSCoW priorities, no NFRs, no UX/error-state coverage, and critically no Open Questions section with named owners and dates -- the closest it comes is prose that explicitly defers the rest-day-rule ownership question to a future confirmation 'before design starts, not assumed here,' which is honest but is also the document admitting, in its own text, that engineering and design cannot proceed without a meeting. That directly undercuts the ask's requirement that the document let engineering size the work and design start sketching without coming back to ask. Guardrail metric is also underspecified: leading indicators are tracked but the document itself says neither is the metric leadership named, so no true guardrail-with-threshold is established. All five probes were still answerable from the text alone, including a clean, explicit answer on the stop condition and top risk. Overall a stronger analytical memo than PRD-as-deliverable; the honesty and stop-condition are real strengths but the missing scopable structure is a genuine defect, not a formatting nitpick.

Template with the {{title}} placeholder left unfilled and every section replaced by generic boilerplate ('relevant stakeholders', 'appropriate owner', 'as appropriate'). None of the scenario's facts appear anywhere -- no Renata Okafor, no 3-4 hour rebuild, no 12% reassignment rate, no DriverGo, no union rest-day rule, no driver or hub counts, no Marcus Feld, no peak-season deadline. Every rubric criterion fails for the same reason: there is no pointable evidence, no named user segment, no measurable goal, no real metric, and the one Open Questions row and one FR row are unfilled placeholders rather than content. Held-out criteria are similarly empty; the 'no internal contradiction' check is only trivially true because there are no concrete claims to contradict each other, which is not a meaningful pass. None of the five probes are answerable from this document -- it does not mention the trucking division, a stop condition, a risky dependency, a specific metric, or an owner of the rest-day rule. This is not a weak PRD, it is an unrendered template.

Rubric detail: problem_weight_and_evidence=5 (Denver anecdote with named scheduler, 3-4hr rebuild, repeat double-booking, 12% reassignment rate, all explicitly marked as evidence vs. inference; Problem section outweighs the solution section); goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=3 (no dedicated Goals section - the outcome goal lives inside Success criteria instead; Out-of-scope entries are strong and reasoned, e.g. the SaaS-vendor-cancellation rationale); target_user_specificity=5 (named schedulers per hub, named sponsor, named situation); metrics_primary_and_guardrail=3 (clear primary metric and window, but no distinct guardrail metric, only 'leading indicators'); open_questions_owned_and_dated=1 (no Open Questions table at all - ownership gaps are raised in prose but never tabled with an owner/date); unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=1 (no functional requirements table, no UX section, nothing to size). Held-out detail: scopable_without_a_meeting=2 (no FR/dependency/NFR rows an engineer could size against, despite rich prose); explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=5 (dedicated Stop condition section names a concrete trigger tied to the peak-season deadline); no_internal_contradiction=5 (no contradiction found across sections); decision_vs_input_traceable=5 (exceptional and repeated: 'we are concluding, not confirmed'; 'we are told... we have not been told who owns'; 'a related opportunity, not a stated requirement' - the document is unusually disciplined about marking inference vs. instruction). All 5 probes answerable: scope exclusion, stop condition, riskiest dependency (DriverGo, explicit), guardrail/metric+deadline, and rest-day-rule owner (hedged as 'most plausible' but named: regional ops managers). Distractors: correctly omits the $50k finance/budget-review fact; the long-haul-trucking mention is the legitimate scope-boundary answer the probe requires, not a distractor violation. Overall: the strongest epistemic reasoning of the three, but it reads as a well-argued memo, not a document engineering could size without a follow-up conversation - it never gives them a requirements list, an NFR, or a dependency table with owner/status, which is the ask's explicit bar.

Every section is generic filler that could describe literally any initiative; the title placeholder ({{title}}) was never even filled in. No fact from the scenario appears anywhere - no drivers, no DriverGo, no Denver, no 12 percent, no union rule, no Marcus Feld. Rubric criteria all score 1: 'Goals' is 'improve the relevant experience... noticeable and valued', non-goals is a blank deferral, target users is 'relevant stakeholders', success metrics is 'expected to trend positively', open questions owner is 'Appropriate owner' / 'As appropriate', and the single FR row is content-free. Held-out: scopable_without_a_meeting=1 (nothing sizeable), explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=1 (none), no_internal_contradiction=2 (trivially non-contradictory only because there is no real content to contradict - this is not a meaningful pass), decision_vs_input_traceable=1 (uniform hedge-voice throughout, no attribution of any kind). Zero of the five probes are answerable from this document alone - a judge reading it in isolation cannot even determine what product or problem is under discussion. This is the clearest case in the set of a document that looks organized (full heading set, tables present) while containing no actual information; per the anti-form instruction this should not be scored any higher for its structure.

Rubric detail: problem_weight_and_evidence=5 (same strong evidence base as A, Problem section longer and more specific than Solution overview); goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=5 (four outcome-phrased goals; three non-goals each with a stated reason, e.g. 'not to design a new swap workflow' vs. 'make swaps visible and recorded'); target_user_specificity=5 (named scheduler role, situation, explicit exclusion of long-haul team); metrics_primary_and_guardrail=5 (primary metric, a distinct guardrail - zero rest-day-rule violations - and a measurement window, all present as separate named lines); open_questions_owned_and_dated=5 (two rows, each with a real owner - regional ops managers, VP of Operations - and a milestone); unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=2 (FR table is fully MoSCoW-tagged, but there is no UX and design section at all, so the empty/loading/error-state half of this criterion is simply absent). Held-out detail: scopable_without_a_meeting=5 (FR rows, NFR targets with numbers, and a dependency table with named owners and status - an engineer could plausibly size this); explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=2 (the document raises the need for a stop condition only as an Open Question owed by the VP before the peak-season checkpoint - it never states the trigger itself, which is a real gap given how directly the ask calls for one); no_internal_contradiction=4 (broadly consistent; one minor tension between 'scheduler trusts it without re-verifying' in Target users and FR2's 'block or flag' language, which implies the scheduler still reviews flagged cases); decision_vs_input_traceable=2 (confident, declarative voice throughout - scope calls like the SaaS-to-build decision and the swap-automation non-goal are stated as settled fact without distinguishing what leadership mandated from what the author chose). 4 of 5 probes answerable: scope exclusion, riskiest dependency, guardrail/metric+deadline, and rest-day-rule owner all land cleanly; the stop-condition probe fails because the document defers that question rather than answering it. Overall: the most complete and structurally scopable of the three - closest to something a senior PM could hand to engineering with minor edits - but it trades away some of the epistemic honesty and the stop-condition commitment that made Artifact A stronger on the held-out, decision-usefulness criteria.

Every section is present but empty: 'relevant stakeholders,' 'appropriate team,' 'as appropriate' recur as placeholders where a real fact, name, number, or date belongs. Problem section has zero evidence (no count, quote, or observed frequency). Goal is a feature-shaped platitude, not an outcome. Target user never gets more specific than 'the relevant stakeholders.' Success metrics name no primary/guardrail values or real window. Open questions row has 'Appropriate owner' / 'As appropriate' where an owner and date belong -- this is the unfilled-placeholder case the rubric explicitly disqualifies. Single FR row is too vague to size or test. No named entities from the scenario appear anywhere (no Denver, no DriverGo, no union rule, no VP), so none of the five probes are answerable from this document alone. This is the anti-form trap made literal: full headings, zero content.

Strong, specific, well-evidenced PRD: named scheduler (Renata Okafor), quantified pain (3-4 hrs, 12% day-of reassignment, twice-repeated error), outcome-phrased goals, three non-goals each with a stated reason, named primary/guardrail/window metrics, an FR table with Must/Should on every row, and a two-row open-questions table with real owners and real milestones. Answers all five probes cleanly, including a concrete rollback trigger in the rollout plan ('revert the pilot hub... if the pilot fails to reduce build time or introduces rest-day violations') that satisfies the stop-condition probe. Two real gaps keep it off a 5: it has no UX and design section at all, so the unhappy-path half of the FR/UX criterion is simply absent despite the strong MoSCoW half; and the prose reports conclusions in a flat, undifferentiated voice, so a reader mostly cannot tell what the author decided versus what a stakeholder handed them (contrast with how explicitly Artifact C marks this). Also recites the long-haul-trucking distractor as a non-goal -- legitimate scoping content, but it is scenario distractor material, not a sign of extra completeness. Dependency rows all say 'Not started,' which is thinner than it looks for actually sizing effort.

The most epistemically careful of the three: it explicitly separates confirmed fact from inference throughout ('we are concluding, not confirmed, that the two are connected'; 'that should be confirmed with them before design starts, not assumed here'; 'a related opportunity, not a stated requirement'). That is exactly the decided-vs-told distinction the held-out criteria look for, and it also carries a dedicated, concrete Stop condition section naming both the metric-miss and the compliance-failure triggers tied explicitly to peak season -- the clearest stop condition of the three documents. Problem section is the strongest of the three: longest, most developed, and honest about which links are inference versus fact. But structurally this reads more like a decision memo than a PRD an engineer or designer could work from unassisted: there is no functional requirements table, no MoSCoW priority anywhere, no NFR targets, no dependency table, no rollout/release plan, and no UX and design section, so unhappy paths are never addressed. Success criteria names a primary metric and window but no separate guardrail metric. The open-question on rule ownership is handled with the same honest hedging as everything else ('most plausible owners... but that should be confirmed'), which is candid but means the document itself concedes it has not closed the gap the ask required ('without coming back to ask what we meant'). Also recites the long-haul-trucking distractor, same as B. Answers all five probes, several (stop condition, risk ranking, decision-vs-input) more precisely than B, but the missing FR/NFR/dependency/rollout scaffolding is exactly what a senior practitioner would flag before this goes to engineering, so it lands below B despite its narrative and epistemic strength.

Strongest of the three on structure and evidence: Problem section names who (Renata Okafor), frequency (weekly, 3-4hr rebuild, 12% quarter reassignment), and cost, and is longer/more developed than Solution overview.
